## Introduction

Recently there has been substantial discussion around the downsides of service oriented architectures and microservice architectures in particular. While only a few years ago, many people readily adopted microservice architectures due to the numerous benefits they provide such as flexibility in the form of independent deployments, clear ownership, improvements in system stability, and better separation of concerns, in recent years people have begun to decry microservices for their tendency to greatly increase complexity, sometimes making even [trivial features](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y8OnoxKotPQ) difficult to build.

As Uber has grown to around 2,200 critical microservices, we experienced these tradeoffs first hand. Over the last two years, Uber has attempted to reduce microservice complexity while still maintaining the benefits of a microservice architecture. With this blog post we hope to introduce our generalized approach to microservice architectures, which we refer to as “Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture” (DOMA).

While it’s been popular in recent years to criticize microservice architectures because of these downsides, few people have advocated an outright rejection of microservice architectures. The operational benefits are too important, and it seems that there are no, or limited, alternatives. **Our goal with DOMA is to provide a way forward for organizations that want to reduce overall system complexity while maintaining the flexibility associated with microservice architectures.**

This piece explains DOMA, the concerns that led to the adoption of this architecture for Uber, its benefits for platform and product teams, and, finally, some advice for teams who want to adopt this architecture. 

## What is a microservice?

Microservices are an extension of service oriented architectures. As opposed to the fairly large “services” of the 2000s, microservices are applications that represent a set of narrowly scoped functionality. These applications are hosted and available over the network and expose a well-defined interface. Other applications call this interface by making a “[remote procedure call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_procedure_call)” (RPC).

The key characteristic of microservice architecture is the way in which code is hosted, called, and deployed. If we think about large, monolithic applications, they are generally split into encapsulated components with well-defined interfaces. These interfaces would then be called directly in-process as opposed to over the network. In this way, we can start to think of a microservice as a library with a performance hit (network I/O and serialization / deserialization) in order to call any of its functions.

When we think about microservices this way, we might question why we would adopt a microservice architecture at all. The answer is often _independent deployments and scaling_. With a large, monolithic application, an organization is forced to deploy or release all of their code at once. Each new version of an application can involve numerous changes. Deployments become risky and time consuming. Anyone can bring the whole system down. 

In other words, organizations adopt microservices for an _operational_ benefit at the expense of _performance_. Organizations also must take on the cost to maintain the infrastructure necessary to support microservices. In many situations, it turns out, this trade-off makes a lot of sense, but it is also a strong argument against a premature adoption of a microservice architecture.

## Motivations

At Uber, we adopted a microservice architecture because we had (circa 2012-2013) primarily two monolithic services and ran into many of the operational issues that microservices solve.

*   **Availability Risks.** A single regression within a monolithic code base can bring the whole system (in this case, all of Uber) down.
*   **Risky, expensive deployments.** These were painful and time consuming to perform with the frequent need for rollbacks.
*   **Poor separation of concerns.** It was difficult to maintain good separations of concerns with a huge code base. In an exponential growth environment, expediency sometimes led to poor boundaries between logic and components.
*   **Inefficient execution.** These issues combined made it difficult for teams to execute autonomously or independently.

In other words, as Uber grew from 10s to 100s of engineers with multiple teams owning pieces of the tech stack, the monolithic architecture tied the fate of teams together and made it difficult to operate independently.

As a result, we adopted a microservice architecture. Ultimately our systems became more _flexible_, which allowed teams to be more _autonomous._

*   **System reliability. Overall system reliability goes up in a microservice architecture. A single service can go down (and be rolled back) without taking down the whole system.**
*   **Separation of concerns.** Architecturally, microservice architectures force you to ask the question “why does this service exist?” more clearly defining the roles of different components.
*   **Clear Ownership. It becomes much clearer who owned what code. Services are typically owned at the individual, team, or org level enabling faster growth.**
*   Autonomous execution. Independent deployments + clearer lines of ownership unlock autonomous execution by various product and platform teams.
*   **Developer Velocity.** Teams can deploy their code independently, which enables them to execute at their own pace.

It’s not an exaggeration to say that Uber would not have been able to accomplish the scale and quality of execution that we maintain today without a microservice architecture.

However, as the company grew even larger, 100s of engineers to 1000s, we began to notice a set of issues associated with greatly increased system _complexity_. With a microservice architecture one trades a single monolithic code base for black boxes whose functionality can change at any time and easily cause unexpected behavior.

For instance, engineers had to work through around 50 services across 12 different teams in order to investigate the root cause of the problem.

Understanding dependencies between services can become quite difficult, as calls between services can go many layers deep. A latency spike in the nth dependency can cause a cascade of issues upstream. Visibility into what’s actually happening is impossible without the right tools, making debugging difficult.  

[![](https://cn-geo1.uber.com/image-proc/resize/udam/format=auto/quality=0/width=2160/REDACTED)](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/43f3a1b3-49a1-53e0-a661-44aa37319c3f.png)

Uber’s microservice architecture circa mid-2018 from Jaeger

In order to build a simple feature an engineer often has to work across multiple services, all of which are owned by different individuals and teams. This requires extensive collaboration with time spent on meetings, design, and code review. The earlier promise of clear lines of service ownership is compromised as teams build code within each other’s services, modify each other’s data models, and even perform deployments on behalf of service owners. Networked monoliths can form, where services that appear to be independent all have to be deployed together to safely perform any change.

[![](https://cn-geo1.uber.com/image-proc/resize/udam/format=auto/quality=0/width=2160/REDACTED)](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/425979e2-8c11-5fcf-85ce-dad321ab6c6a.png)

An example of a complex flow at Uber circa 2018, which required 10 touch points for a simple integration before DOMA.

The result is a slower developer experience, instability for service owners, more painful migrations, etc. For organizations that have already adopted a microservice architecture there is no turning back. It becomes a case of “_can’t live with them, can’t live without them_.” 

## Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture

If we can think of microservices as I/O bound libraries and a “microservice architecture” as a large, distributed application then we can use well understood architectures to think about how to organize our code. 

“Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture” thus draws heavily from established ways to organize code such as [Domain-driven Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-driven_design), [Clean Architecture](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html), [Service-Oriented Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service-oriented_architecture), and object- and interface-oriented design patterns. **We think of DOMA as innovative only insofar as it is a relatively novel way to leverage established design principles in large distributed systems in large organizations.**

The core principles and terminology associated with DOMA are as follows:

1.  Instead of orienting around single microservices, we oriented around collections of related microservices. We call these **domains.**
2.  We further create collections of domains which we call layers. The layer that the domain belongs to establishes what dependencies the microservices within that domain are allowed to take on. We call this **layer design.**
3.  We provide clean interfaces for domains that we treat as a single point of entry into the collection. We call these **gateways.**
4.  Finally, we establish that _each domain should be agnostic to other domains,_ which is to say, a domain shouldn’t have logic related to another domain hard coded inside of its code base or data models. Since frequently teams do need to include logic in another team’s domain (for example, custom validation logic or some meta context on a data model), we provide an **extension architecture** to support well defined extension points within the domain.

In other words, by providing a systematic architecture, domain gateways, and predefined extension points, DOMA intends to transform microservice architectures from something complex to something comprehensible: a structured set of flexible, reusable, and layered components. 

The rest of this post digs into Uber’s implementation of DOMA, the benefits we’ve seen, and practical advice for companies which might want to adopt this approach.

## Uber’s Implementation

### Domains

Uber domains represent a collection of one or more microservices tied to a logical grouping of functionality. A common question in designing a domain is “how big should a domain be?” We give no guidance here. Some domains can include tens of services, some domains only a single service. The important task is to think carefully about the _logical_ role of each collection. For instance, our map search services constitute a domain, fare services are a domain, matching platform (matching riders and drivers) are a domain. These also don’t always follow company org structure. The Uber Maps org itself is split into three domains, with 80 microservices behind 3 different gateways.

### Layer Design

Layer design answers the question of “what service can call what other service?” within Uber’s microservice architecture. As a result, we can think of layer design as “separation of concerns at scale.” Alternatively, we can think of layer design as “dependency management at scale.” 

Layer design describes a mechanism for thinking about failure blast radius and product specificity across service dependencies at Uber. _As domains move from the bottom layer to the top layer, they impact fewer services in the case of an outage and represent more specific product use cases._ Conversely, functionality at the bottom layers have more dependents and as a result tend to have a larger blast radius and represent a more general set of business functionality. The figure below illustrates this concept.

[](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/3046e113-a661-56cf-9c19-a145c008843c.png)

[![](https://cn-geo1.uber.com/image-proc/resize/udam/format=auto/quality=0/width=2160/REDACTED)](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/3046e113-a661-56cf-9c19-a145c008843c.png)

One can think of the top layers as specific user experiences (such as mobile features), and the bottom layers as generalized business functionality (such as account management or marketplace trips). Layers only depend on the layers under them, which gives us a useful heuristic to think about questions like blast radius and domain integration.

It’s worth noting that functionality often moves “down” this chart from specific to more general. One can imagine a simple feature that eventually becomes more and more of a platform as requirements evolve. In fact, this sort of migration downward is expected, and many of Uber’s core business platforms started as rider or driver specific functionality that became more generalized as we developed more lines of business and they took on more dependencies (such as Uber Eats or Uber Freight).

Within Uber, we established the following five layers.

1.  **Infrastructure layer.** Provides functionality that any engineering organization could use. It’s Uber’s answer to the big engineering questions, such as storage or networking.
2.  **Business layer.** Provides functionality that Uber as an organization could use, but that is not specific to a particular product category or line of business (LOB) such as Rides, Eats, or Freight.
3.  **Product layer.** Provides functionality that relates to a particular product category or LOB, but is agnostic to the mobile application, such as the “request a ride” logic which is leveraged by multiple Rides facing applications (Rider, Rider “Lite”, m.uber.com, etc).
4.  **Presentation.** Provide functionality that directly relates to features that exist within a consumer-facing application (mobile/web). 
5.  **Edge Layer.** Safely exposes Uber services to the outside world. This layer is also mobile application aware.

As you can see, each subsequent layer represents an increasingly specific grouping of functionality, and has a smaller and smaller blast radius (or, in other words, less components depend on the functionality within that layer). 

### Gateways

The term “Gateway API” is already a [broadly established](https://www.redhat.com/en/topics/api/what-does-an-api-gateway-do) concept within microservice architectures. Our definition does not vary greatly from the established definition, except that we tend to think of gateways exclusively as a **single entry-point** into a collection of underlying services, which we call a **domain.** The success of a gateway relies on the success of the API design.

[![](https://cn-geo1.uber.com/image-proc/resize/udam/format=auto/quality=0/width=2160/REDACTED)](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/c6e95c28-223a-52d1-a431-249d1706bcd2.png)

The following figure illustrates the high level diagram of a gateway. It abstracts away the internal details of the domains – multiple services, data tables, ETL pipelines etc. Only the interfaces – RPC APIs, messaging events and queries are exposed to other domains.

Since upstream consumers only operate on a single service, gateways provide numerous benefits in terms of **future migrations,** **discoverability,** and overall reduction in **system complexity** with upstream services only taking a single dependency as opposed to dependencies on several downstream services that might exist within a domain. If we think about gateways in the sense of OO design, they are interface definitions, which enable us to do whatever we want in terms of the underlying “implementation” (in this case the collection of underlying microservices).

### Extensions

Extensions represent a mechanism to _extend_ domains. The basic definition of an extension is that it provides a mechanism for extending the functionality of an underlying service without changing the actual implementation of that service and without impacting its overall reliability. At Uber we provide two different extension models: **logic extensions** and **data extensions**. The concept of extensions has allowed us to scale our architecture to multiple teams being able to work independently of each other.

#### Logic Extensions

Logic extensions provide a mechanism for extending the underlying logic of a service. For logic extensions we use a variation of a _provider_ or _plugin_ pattern with an interface defined on a service-by-service basis. This makes it so that extending teams can implement extension logic in an interface-driven way without modifying the core code of the underlying platform.

For example, a driver goes online. Typically, we make various checks to ensure that a driver is allowed to go online (safety checks, compliance, etc.). Each of these is owned by an individual team. One way to implement this would be to have each team write logic in the same endpoint, but this can introduce complexity. Each check would require custom, and entirely unrelated, logic. 

In the case of logic extensions, the “go online” endpoint would define an interface that they expect each extension to conform to with a predefined request type and a response. Each team would register an extension that would be responsible for the execution of this logic. In this case, they might simply take some context about the driver and return a bool, saying if the driver can go online or not. The go online endpoint would simply iterate through these responses, and determine if any of them are false.

This decouples the core code from each extension, and provides isolation between extensions, which don’t know what other logic is executing. It’s easy to build up more functionality around this, such as observability or feature flagging. 

#### Data Extensions

Data extensions provide a mechanism for attaching arbitrary data to an interface to avoid bloat in core platform data models. For data extensions, we leverage Protobuf’s [Any](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#any) functionality so that teams can add arbitrary data to requests. Services will often store this data or pass it to a logic extension so that the core platform is never responsible for deserializing (and thus “knowing about”) this arbitrary context. Protobuf’s Any implementation comes with some infrastructure overhead in exchange for stronger typing. For a simpler implementation, one could just as easily use a JSON string to represent arbitrary data.

[](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/3cc2d61d-d571-53e4-b832-c9a18765aadd.png)

[![](https://cn-geo1.uber.com/image-proc/resize/udam/format=auto/quality=0/width=2160/REDACTED)](https://tb-static.uber.com/prod/udam-assets/3cc2d61d-d571-53e4-b832-c9a18765aadd.png)

#### Custom

Outside of logic and data extensions, many teams at Uber have introduced their own extension patterns that are appropriate for their domain. For example, much of the integrations tied to our presentation architecture uses DAG based task execution logic.

## Benefits

Almost every major domain at Uber has been influenced on some level by DOMA. Over the last year, we have focused primarily on Uber’s business layer which provides generalized logic for each of our various lines of business. 

DOMA is still young at Uber, and we are excited to share more data and in-depth examples of our architecture in the future. However, early signs have been extremely positive in terms of a simplified developer experience and a reduction in overall system complexity.

### Products & Platforms

DOMA was the result of a consensus effort across product and platform teams at Uber. Platform support costs often dropped an order of magnitude. Product teams benefited from guard rails and accelerated development.  
  
For example, an early platform consumer of our extensions architecture was able to drop the time to prioritize and integrate a new feature from three days to three hours by adopting an extension architecture with reduced time for code review, planning, and learning curve for consumers.

### Reduced Complexity

Previously product teams would have to call numerous downstream services to leverage a domain; they now have to call just one. By reducing the number of touchpoints to onboard a new feature, platforms were able to reduce onboarding time by 25-50%. Furthermore, we were able to classify 2200 microservices into 70 domains. Roughly 50% of which have been implemented, and most of which have some plan for future adoption.

### Future Migrations 

At Uber, we calculated that the half-life of a microservice was 1.5 years, which means that every 1.5 years 50% of our microservices churn. Without gateways it’s easy for a microservice architecture to fall into a “migration hell” as a result of this churn. Ever changing microservices constantly require upstream migrations. Gateways enable teams to avoid dependencies on the underlying domain services, which means those services can change without forcing an upstream migration. 

Two of Uber’s largest platform rewrites in the last year happened behind gateways. These platforms had hundreds of services that depended on them that would have had to migrate existing consumers. The cost of migration in these cases would have been extremely high, making a complete platform rewrite infeasible.

### New Lines of Business & Products

Platforms designed using DOMA have proven to be much more extensible and easier to maintain. Most teams at Uber who adopted DOMA did so because supporting new lines of business had become too expensive.

## Practical Advice

This section provides some practical advice for companies that might want to adopt DOMA. The guiding principle here is that in our experience a mature and thoughtful microservice architecture stems from quiet nudges in the right direction at the right time. The reality is that a true “rewrite” is never possible for one’s entire microservice architecture.

As a result, we think of evolving a microservice architecture more like “trimming a hedge” so that it eventually grows correctly, rather than a top-down or one-time architecture (or re-architecture) effort. It’s a dynamic and progressive process.

### Startups

The driving questions should be “when should we adopt a microservice architecture?” and “does it make sense for our organization?” As we’ve seen above, while microservices provide an operational benefit to organizations with a large number of engineers, this trades off with an increase in complexity that can make features more difficult to build.

In small organizations, the operational benefit likely does not offset the increase in architectural complexity. Furthermore, microservice architectures often require dedicated engineering resources to support which may be out of budget for an early stage company or else suboptimal from a prioritization perspective. 

With this in mind, it isn’t unreasonable to hold off on microservices altogether for some time. If an organization does choose to adopt microservices, it should think about the “microservice as large distributed application” analogy, and the separation of concerns between microservices it wants to build. Also, recognize that the first microservices will likely be the most important and longest lasting as they truly describe the core of the business.

### Midsize

Once a company becomes midsized with multiple teams and the clear separation of concerns becomes hazy between different features and platforms, microservice architectures become more obviously useful.

It’s at this stage that one can begin to think about hierarchies between microservices. Dependency management may become more important, as some services begin to become more obviously critical to business operation, and more and more teams rely on them. 

Early investment in platformization may pay dividends down the road. There is the possibility to avoid tech debt here if one can create completely product agnostic business platforms and avoid arbitrary product logic in core platform services. It might make sense to adopt extensions at this point to accomplish that goal.

Given that the number of microservices is likely still quite low, it may not make sense to cluster them together. However, it’s worth noting here that a domain in the context of Uber’s DOMA implementation can contain a single service, so it may still be useful to think in a “domain-oriented” way.

### Large

Larger engineering organizations may have hundreds of engineers and microservices and several dependencies. At this point DOMA reaches its full usefulness. There will likely be obvious clusters of microservices that can be easily grouped together into domains with a gateway in front of them. Legacy services often begin to need to be refactored or rewritten and then migrated, which means that gateways will soon begin to provide value in terms of ease of migration if they are already in place.

Clear hierarchy will also become increasingly important with some services operating as “product” services for particular features or grouping of features, and other services will increasingly support multiple products and be thought of as “platforms.” It’s critical at this stage to keep arbitrary product logic decoupled from platforms, so as to avoid a heavy operational burden on platform teams as well as system-wide instability.

## Final Thoughts

We are still actively evolving DOMA as more and more teams at Uber come to adopt it. The critical insight of DOMA is that a microservice architecture is really just one, large, distributed program and you can apply the same principles to its evolution that you would apply to any piece of software. DOMA is simply an approach for thinking about these principles in practice. We hope others find it useful and we look forward to feedback!

DOMA itself was the result of a cross-functional effort, which involved nearly 60 engineers across every org at Uber. Some particular acknowledgements, for people who invested heavily into this effort over the last 2 years…

Acknowledgements:

This work brings multiple existing design patterns in the industry to solve problems at Uber while also suggesting new patterns like extensions. We are thankful to the industry for the work on them. We are also thankful to the engineers at Linkedin who worked on [Superblocks](https://engineering.linkedin.com/architecture/brief-history-scaling-linkedin), who spoke to us about their experiences.

# Platform-service development mocks

## Summary

SystemHost declarations will model shared platform services as external Dapr app identities used by individual integration components. An optional, separate development definition will resolve selected services to OpenAPI-backed mocks. During local SystemHost runs, one Microcks instance will host those mocks and generated Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` resources will transparently redirect existing service-invocation calls to Microcks.

Integration projects, platform-service implementations, client configuration, and production Dapr app IDs remain unchanged.

## Context

Intropy integration components use Dapr service invocation to call two shared platform services:

- `idempotency-service`
- `business-incident-service`

The externally inspected Entrovia order-flow workspace—not this repository's minimal `examples/OrderFlow.*` projects—confirms the relevant behavior:

- both `order-extractor` and `order-loader` use both services;
- both components retain the client packages' default Dapr app IDs;
- the framework calls `POST /status` and `POST /commit` on the idempotency service;
- the framework calls `POST /events` with structured CloudEvents to trigger or resolve business incidents;
- each component already carries local `HTTPEndpoint` resources with the production app IDs as `metadata.name` values;
- those endpoints currently target locally hosted real services with their databases, messaging, migrations, and Dapr sidecars.

The existing component overlay gives the SystemHost a clean substitution point: generated resources replace component-local resources with the same `metadata.name` when staging each sidecar's effective Dapr resource set.

Dapr resolves a named `HTTPEndpoint` before app-ID discovery. A development resource named `idempotency-service` therefore satisfies an unchanged invocation of `/v1.0/invoke/idempotency-service/method/status` while forwarding it to Microcks.

## Goals

- Make platform-service dependencies visible in the topology.
- Preserve existing integration code, client configuration, and service invocation paths.
- Scope each generated mock endpoint to the components that declared the dependency.
- Keep development substitutions separate from the environment-independent system topology.
- Run one lightweight Microcks instance for all declared OpenAPI mocks.
- Keep mock behavior stateless and contract-backed in the first version.
- Preserve deterministic generation and the existing component-overlay model.
- Fail before integration startup when a declared mock is missing, invalid, or cannot be imported. Behavioral completeness is enforced by compatibility tests rather than inferred from contract identity alone.

## Non-goals

- Deploying the real platform services.
- Changing either platform service or its client package.
- Stateful idempotency behavior, duplicate history, or incident lifecycle emulation.
- Scenario switching, latency injection, or failure injection.
- Falling back from a mock to a real service.
- Mocking Dapr pub/sub, bindings, or arbitrary external systems.
- Replacing standalone component development commands; they continue using their own local Dapr resources unless addressed separately.
- Generating Kubernetes workloads for platform services or Microcks.

## Design principles

### Dependencies are identities

A platform-service dependency is identified by the Dapr app ID that callers already invoke. It does not contain an image, port, Helm chart, or local implementation.

### Usage is component-scoped

Dependencies are edges from a component to an external platform service. Per-component declarations support accurate topology graphs, narrow Dapr scopes, and startup dependencies without coupling unrelated components.

### Development resolution is separate

The system topology records that a component uses a service. An optional development definition records that local runs resolve that service to an OpenAPI mock. Microcks does not appear in the public DSL; the local generation and Aspire backends jointly implement the Microcks URL and lifecycle contract.

### The adapter is unnecessary

A Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` already preserves the caller-facing service invocation API and can contain the full Microcks service/version base path. A proxy adapter would add processes, sidecars, readiness, and forwarding semantics without changing the result.

## Proposed DSL

### Platform-service references

SystemHosts declare reusable service references alongside topics and connectors:

```csharp
using Intropy.Topology;

public static class Services
{
    public static readonly ServiceRef Idempotency =
        ServiceRef.Define("idempotency-service");

    public static readonly ServiceRef BusinessIncidents =
        ServiceRef.Define("business-incident-service");
}
```

`ServiceRef` contains one value: `AppId`. The value is validated as a DNS-1123 label when the reference is created.

### Component usage

Every component builder exposes `.Uses(ServiceRef)` and returns its concrete builder type:

```csharp
public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
{
    builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor")
        .From(Connectors.OrderExtractorSource)
        .Publishes(Topics.Order)
        .Uses(Services.Idempotency)
        .Uses(Services.BusinessIncidents)
        .WithSchedule("* * * * *");

    builder.AddLoader("order-loader")
        .Subscribes(Topics.Order)
        .To(Connectors.OrderLoaderDestination)
        .Uses(Services.Idempotency)
        .Uses(Services.BusinessIncidents);
}
```

The declaration describes connectivity only. It does not imply that the SystemHost owns or deploys the provider.

### Separate development definition

Development substitutions live in a separate discoverable type:

```csharp
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;

public sealed class OrderFlowDevelopment : IDevelopmentDefinition
{
    public void Define(DevelopmentBuilder development)
    {
        development.Mock(Services.Idempotency)
            .FromOpenApi("mocks/idempotency-service.openapi.yaml");

        development.Mock(Services.BusinessIncidents)
            .FromOpenApi("mocks/business-incident-service.openapi.yaml");
    }
}
```

Artifact paths are relative to the SystemHost project directory: `builder.AppHostDirectory` during Aspire runs and the command's current working directory for `check` and `generate`. The canonical tasks already execute commands from that directory. Backends canonicalize the root and resolved artifact path before validation; published SystemHosts and invocation from an unrelated working directory are outside this local-development contract.

OpenAPI `info.title` and `info.version` determine the Microcks service identity and URL. The DSL does not repeat those values.

The expected SystemHost layout is:

```text
order-flow/
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs
├── OrderFlowDevelopment.cs
├── Services.cs
└── mocks/
    ├── idempotency-service.openapi.yaml
    └── business-incident-service.openapi.yaml
```

## Core topology model

`ServiceRef` belongs to `Intropy.Topology` because service usage is part of the environment-independent topology.

Conceptually, each materialized component gains its used app IDs:

```csharp
public sealed record ComponentModel
{
    public required IReadOnlyList<string> Uses { get; init; }
}
```

The topology also exposes resources derived from those edges:

```csharp
public sealed record ServiceResource
{
    public required string AppId { get; init; }
    public required IReadOnlyList<string> Consumers { get; init; }
}
```

`SystemTopology.Services` is sorted by app ID. `Consumers` is unique and sorted. Component declaration order remains unchanged.

As with topics and connectors, service resources materialize from usage. There is no system-level `AddService` or `UsesService` method.

## Development model and discovery

Development types belong to `Intropy.Topology.Generation`, keeping local-runtime concerns out of the core topology package.

The generation package provides:

- `IDevelopmentDefinition`
- `DevelopmentBuilder`
- an immutable development manifest
- development-definition discovery
- validation of mock declarations and artifacts

Discovery rules:

1. The assembly must still contain exactly one `ISystemDefinition`.
2. The assembly may contain zero or one concrete `IDevelopmentDefinition`.
3. The system topology is built before the development definition.
4. The development builder receives the validated topology so it can reject unknown or unused service references.
5. No development definition means no generated service mocks and no Microcks resource.

The separate development type keeps generated or regenerated system declarations focused on topology and lets local configuration evolve independently.

## OpenAPI contract handling

The development manifest records the service app ID and resolved artifact path. Contract inspection extracts:

- OpenAPI version;
- `info.title`;
- `info.version`.

The first version accepts self-contained OpenAPI 3.0.x documents. Missing identity fields, external `$ref` dependencies, and unsupported document versions fail validation. Broader OpenAPI support is added only when a concrete contract requires it and the pinned Microcks release supports it.

Microcks URLs are built in one internal abstraction from the imported identity. SystemHost authors do not encode Microcks paths or title escaping.

The first order-flow mock contracts are deliberately narrow overlays matching actual client traffic rather than copies of the full upstream API documents.

### Idempotency mock

Required operations:

```text
POST /status → 200
{"action":"Proceed","reason":"NoPreviousData"}

POST /commit → 200 with an empty body
```

The mock always allows processing and accepts every commit. It does not retain state.

### Business-incident mock

Required operation:

```text
POST /events → 202 with an empty response body
Request Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json
```

The same operation accepts triggered and resolved structured CloudEvents. The mock does not persist or expose incidents.

The contracts select their single happy-path response independently of request-body values. They include the OpenAPI examples and Microcks associations required for bodyless responses by the pinned Microcks version. Compatibility tests exercise randomized idempotency values and both CloudEvent types so an accidentally body-sensitive dispatcher cannot pass.

## Generated Dapr resources

Generation accepts the validated topology and optional development manifest. It emits one `HTTPEndpoint` for each mocked service.

Conceptually:

```yaml
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: HTTPEndpoint
metadata:
  name: idempotency-service
spec:
  baseUrl: http://localhost:8585/rest/<encoded-title>/<encoded-version>
scopes:
- order-extractor
- order-loader
```

Generation rules:

- `metadata.name` is the service app ID.
- `spec.baseUrl` is derived from the imported OpenAPI identity.
- `scopes` contains exactly the service's consumers, sorted ordinally.
- Output is deterministic and one resource is emitted per mocked service.
- An unmocked service emits no `HTTPEndpoint`; normal Dapr discovery or a component-local resource remains in effect.
- Although the generated artifact is system-level, staging copies a mock endpoint only into overlays for its declared consumers. A non-consumer's same-named local endpoint is left untouched.
- Replacement requires the resource identity `(apiVersion, kind, metadata.name)` to match. Duplicate identities, multi-document files, or a same-name resource of another kind fail staging rather than deleting an ambiguous file.
- Mock resources belong only to the repository's existing local-run generation path. Kubernetes generation is outside this design.

The current `generate` command already emits backend-dependent local resources, such as Redis endpoints, without starting their backends. Development mock endpoints follow the same rule: generated output is a manifest for the local runtime, not a standalone runnable stack. When a development definition exists, its endpoints are included so command output and Aspire staging use the same generated truth.

## Aspire lifecycle

The Aspire backend starts Microcks only when at least one mock is declared.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[Discover and validate topology] --> D[Discover and validate development definition]
    D --> G[Generate Dapr resources]
    D --> M[Start one Microcks instance]
    M --> I[Import OpenAPI artifacts]
    I --> V[Verify imported service identities]
    G --> S[Stage consumer-specific Dapr overlays]
    V --> R[Mark each imported mock ready]
    S --> A[Start scoped integration sidecars and apps]
    R --> A
```

Lifecycle requirements:

1. Microcks uses one pinned image version and one fixed host endpoint known to generated Dapr resources.
2. Container health is necessary but not sufficient. Each mock has its own task-backed readiness signal that completes after its artifact has been imported and its Microcks service identity is addressable.
3. Only components consuming a mocked service wait for that service's readiness signal.
4. Their Dapr sidecars are held before startup until Redis and their consumed mocks are ready.
5. Sidecar recovery uses a sidecar-to-readiness mapping rather than one global mock gate.
6. The scheduler awaits the component's readiness set at the start of every cron or **Run now** trigger, even when its sidecar is already running.
7. Import or verification failure marks that service's readiness as failed with the service app ID and artifact path in the error.
8. Static validation completes for all mock declarations before any runtime resource starts; a statically invalid mock prevents every integration from starting.
9. The Aspire dashboard exposes Microcks as one infrastructure resource.

The fixed port is checked before startup and produces a focused error when unavailable. Port configurability is deferred until there is a demonstrated conflict that cannot be handled operationally.

## CLI behavior

### `check`

- Validates the system topology.
- Discovers and validates the optional development definition.
- Verifies artifact existence and OpenAPI identity without starting Microcks.
- Normalizes topology, discovery, file, and parser failures into focused diagnostics and a non-zero exit code without a stack trace by default.

### `graph`

- Includes service usage in the environment-independent topology graph.
- Does not include development mock paths or Microcks details.

A component entry lists its used service app IDs, and the graph's resource projection lists each service and its consumers.

### `generate`

- Generates the existing local Dapr resources and runtime configuration.
- Includes development `HTTPEndpoint` resources when a development definition exists.
- Does not start Microcks or import artifacts; like existing Redis-backed output, the files require the matching local runtime backend.

### `run`

- Performs all checks above.
- Starts Microcks, imports and verifies contracts, stages generated endpoints, and then starts consumers.

`Program.cs` remains unchanged because both backends continue discovering definitions from the SystemHost assembly.

## Validation

### Topology validation

- Service app IDs must be valid DNS-1123 labels.
- A component cannot use the same service more than once.
- Service consumers must be declared topology components.
- A service app ID cannot collide with a topology component app ID.
- Service resources must have at least one consumer by construction.

### Development validation

- At most one development definition may exist.
- A mocked service must occur in the built topology.
- A service may have at most one mock declaration.
- A mock artifact path must resolve within or beneath the canonical SystemHost project directory; `..` traversal and symlink escape are rejected.
- The artifact must exist, be readable, self-contained, and contain an OpenAPI 3.0.x document with non-empty title and version.
- Two different mocked services cannot accidentally resolve to the same Microcks service identity unless explicit aliasing is designed later.
- A development definition may leave a used service unmocked; existing Dapr discovery or component-local resources remain valid resolution mechanisms.

Validation messages identify the component or service app ID and the conflicting declaration. Development discovery, file, and parser failures use one normalized validation result consumed consistently by `check`, `generate`, and `run`. No new public diagnostic-code scheme is introduced by this design.

## Compatibility and migration

The feature is additive:

- integration source code does not change;
- client package registration does not change;
- platform-service source code does not change;
- production app IDs do not change;
- existing component-local Dapr resources remain valid for standalone runs;
- SystemHosts without service declarations or development definitions behave as before.

For order-flow, generated mock endpoints use the same names as the existing local endpoints. The established overlay rule replaces those files only during SystemHost runs. Standalone component runs continue targeting the real local services until a separate standalone-development design is adopted.

## Testing strategy

### Core topology tests

- Every component builder supports fluent `.Uses`.
- Usage materializes deterministic component edges and service resources.
- Duplicate usage and app-ID collisions fail validation.
- Graph serialization includes services and consumers without development data.

### Development discovery tests

- Zero or one development definition is accepted.
- Multiple definitions fail with their type names.
- Unknown, unused, duplicate, missing, escaping, and malformed artifacts fail clearly.
- OpenAPI title and version are extracted from self-contained 3.0.x documents; external references and other versions fail clearly.

### Generation tests

- Exact `HTTPEndpoint` YAML snapshots cover name, base URL, escaping, scopes, and ordering.
- Unmocked services produce no endpoint.
- Generated endpoints replace component-local `HTTPEndpoint` resources by full resource identity during staging.
- Mixed consumer/non-consumer staging proves a non-consumer's same-named local endpoint is preserved.
- Duplicate identities, different-kind collisions, and multi-document resources fail without deleting files.
- Repeated generation is byte-identical.

### Aspire model tests

- No mocks means no Microcks resource or readiness dependency.
- Multiple mocks share one Microcks resource.
- Only consumers wait for Microcks.
- Consumer sidecars are gated on contract-import readiness.
- Import failures prevent component startup.
- Every scheduled or **Run now** trigger awaits readiness even when the sidecar is already running.

### Live compatibility test

An opt-in repository-owned compatibility fixture runs the published platform-service clients through real Dapr sidecars against Microcks and proves:

- idempotency status deserializes to `Proceed / NoPreviousData`;
- commit receives an empty `200`;
- triggered and resolved structured CloudEvents receive `202`;
- client app-ID configuration remains at its defaults.

The external Entrovia order-flow workspace provides the final end-to-end acceptance run; it is not assumed to be available to this repository's CI.

## Acceptance criteria

- The order-flow SystemHost can run both components without starting either real platform service or its backing infrastructure.
- Existing invocations to `idempotency-service` and `business-incident-service` succeed through Dapr without integration changes.
- The generated endpoints are scoped to `order-extractor` and `order-loader`.
- A valid order flows through extractor and loader with stateless idempotency responses.
- A validation failure can be routed to the business-incident mock and acknowledged successfully.
- Missing, invalid, or unimportable contracts fail before either integration starts; semantically incomplete contracts fail the compatibility lane.
- SystemHosts without development mocks retain current behavior.

## Alternatives considered

### Dapr-enabled proxy adapters

Rejected for the first version. They preserve app IDs but add one process and sidecar per service, proxy correctness, and additional readiness concerns. `HTTPEndpoint` provides the required transparent substitution directly.

### System-wide service declarations

Rejected. They hide actual consumers, broaden Dapr scopes, and couple unrelated components to mock readiness.

### Manual endpoint YAML in every component

Rejected as the SystemHost solution. Order-flow demonstrates that it works technically, but it duplicates environment configuration across components and cannot centrally import or gate contracts.

### Microcks-specific DSL

Rejected. The declaration expresses an OpenAPI-backed mock; the local generation and Aspire backends currently fulfil it with Microcks. This keeps tool choice out of the public topology surface while acknowledging the backend contract.

### Full upstream contracts

Rejected for the first version. The inspected upstream artifacts contain operations not used by order-flow and do not fully represent the client traffic needed here. Narrow mock overlays are easier to verify and maintain.

## Risks and mitigations

- **Microcks URL conventions may change.** Keep URL construction in one internal abstraction and pin the Microcks version.
- **OpenAPI mocks may drift from released clients.** Exercise the published clients in an opt-in Dapr/Microcks compatibility test.
- **A mock may conceal a broken production operation.** Keep mocks limited to known client traffic and do not claim production-service conformance from local mock success.
- **Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` remains a `v1alpha1` resource.** Pin and test the supported Dapr runtime range.
- **A fixed Microcks port prevents concurrent local hosts and has a check-to-bind race.** Match the repository's existing fixed-backend-port model for the first version, report focused conflicts, and revisit configurable or allocated ports when concurrent hosts become a requirement.
- **Contract import can lag behind container health.** Gate consumers on verified artifact availability, not container state alone.

## Planning handoff

Implementation planning should determine:

- the OpenAPI 3.0.x parsing dependency;
- the pinned Microcks integration package and image versions from current official documentation;
- the concrete task-backed import and identity-verification mechanism exposed by that Microcks version, including timeout and cancellation behavior;
- the smallest extension of the existing readiness interfaces that supports a sidecar-to-readiness mapping;
- the exact topology graph wire-format evolution and compatibility policy.

The live Dapr/Microcks compatibility test remains opt-in because it requires Docker and initialized Dapr.

These choices must preserve the DSL, lifecycle, scope boundaries, and observable behavior defined above.

## References

- [Dapr: invoke non-Dapr endpoints](https://docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/service-invocation/howto-invoke-non-dapr-endpoints/)
- [Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` specification](https://docs.dapr.io/reference/resource-specs/httpendpoints-schema/)
- [Microcks OpenAPI conventions](https://microcks.io/documentation/references/artifacts/openapi-conventions/)
- [Microcks dispatching rules](https://microcks.io/documentation/explanations/dispatching/)

# 0009: Reduce the library to the minimal model the system tutorial requires

> Status: implemented (2026-07-25).

**Background.** The library had grown a surface well ahead of what any consumer exercised. The
system tutorial (the devex design instrument for this library) and `intropy sys create` — the two
things that actually consume the DSL today — need exactly three block kinds, one topic per
publisher, and file connectors. Everything beyond that was speculative: designed carefully, tested,
and used by nobody. Unused surface is not free — every rule, transport, and builder member is
something the tutorial's reader can wander into, something the CLI templates must not accidentally
depend on, and something each subsequent change must keep consistent.

**Decision.** Cut the library to the minimal model, on the deterministic-over-complexity principle:
keep only what the tutorial and `intropy sys create` demonstrably require; surface the rest as an
explicit gap rather than carrying it speculatively.

What was cut:

- **Aggregator** — the block kind, its builder, and its component subclass.
- **APIs** — `ApiRef<T>`, `Provides`/`Consumes`, `ApiResource`, and ITP501.
- **Named publish ports** — `Publishes(port, topic)`; a component now publishes at most one topic,
  and ITP101 re-purposes from port collisions to "more than one `Publishes` call is an error".
- **Non-file transports** — `Transport.Http()`/`Sftp()`/`Blob()`/`Custom(...)` and the direction
  capability model behind them (ITP105/ITP106). The single remaining transport,
  `Transport.File(rootPath)` (`bindings.localstorage`), reads and writes, so capabilities check
  nothing.
- **Unresolved connectors and `ExternalSystem`** — `ConnectorRef.Define(name, transport)` is the
  only overload; ITP107 retires with the resolution lifecycle (ADR 0007's deferral mechanics go
  with it; its progressive-resolution stance survives as the file-transport default). A file
  connector's folder is its endpoint, so no external-system concept is needed.
- **Dev mocking** — the `IDevProfile` seam and the Microcks integration (ADR 0006's machinery);
  the Aspire backend runs only the dev broker (Redis), projects, and sidecars.
- **The Prod generation profile** — `TopologyGenerator.Generate(topology)` takes no profile; the
  verbs are `check | graph | generate [dir]` with no `--profile`.

Retired diagnostic codes — ITP105, ITP106, ITP107, ITP501 — join ITP201–205 in the never-reuse
list.

**Why now.** The tutorial is the forcing function: it must present a surface a reader can hold in
their head, and the CLI templates must compile against exactly what they generate. Trimming after
the fact is cheaper than explaining, testing, and template-proofing features nothing uses. This is
the same call as the CLI's local-first normalization: borrow what reliably works, cut the rest,
and record the gap.

**The full model is preserved, not deleted.** The pre-cut library lives on the **`full-topology`**
branch. When a cut feature is validated by a real need, re-adding it starts from a cherry-pick or
merge of that branch — not a rewrite. The branch carries the tested implementation, the validation
rules, and the snapshot expectations; reimplementing from memory would rediscover its bugs one at
a time.

## Mechanics

- `Components.cs`, `Building/ComponentBuilders.cs`, `Refs.cs`, and the model records dropped the
  cut members; `SystemTopology` is `{ SystemName, Components, Topics, Connectors }`.
- `ConnectorResource` is `{ Name, Transport (non-null), DaprComponentName (derived), Directions,
  UsedBy }`.
- The example became `examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost` (order-extractor + order-loader +

- The byte-exact JSON snapshot in `EndToEndTests` was regenerated for the reduced model.

- **Async edges** (`Publishes`/`Subscribes` — topics)
- **External-world edges** (`From`/`To` — connectors)
- **Service identities** (`Uses` — `ServiceRef`)

What's missing is a *first-class, contract-carrying, synchronous entry-point into the system* — the "front door." That's exactly what a gateway is, and exactly what `Provides`/`Consumes` was reaching for before it was cut.

## The key improvement over the old design

The old design made the API a **typed ref with provider/consumer edges** — but the *contract* was implicit in the type parameter `T`, and the mocking seam (`IDevProfile`) was a separate concern bolted on later (ADR 0006).

What you're proposing unifies them, and that's the genuinely good idea here: **an API is defined by its contract, and the contract is either `http` (OpenAPI) or `asyncapi`.** That is precisely the pattern the `platform-service-development-mocks` design already proves out with `idempotency-service` / `business-incident-service`:

The mock becomes a degenerate case of "provide an API whose backing implementation is a contract-only stub."

So the DSL shape roughly becomes:

```csharp

    ApiRef.Define("orders-api").FromOpenApi("contracts/orders.openapi.yaml");
    // or .FromAsyncApi("contracts/orders.asyncapi.yaml")

// in the system:
builder.AddApi(Orders)              // the gateway / single entry-point
    .HandledBy(Components.OrderLoader);  // which internal component serves it

// consumers reference the ApiRef, never the internal component
```

1. **It gives the system a real boundary.** Today anything can reach any component. A gateway-API makes "what does this system expose to the outside" an explicit, graphable, contract-backed declaration — the DOMA "single point of entry" benefit.
2. **It reuses proven machinery instead of inventing new.** The OpenAPI validation, identity extraction, Microcks import, and `HTTPEndpoint` substitution all already exist in the mocks design. Adding `FromAsyncApi` extends it to the messaging side, which the current mocks don't cover.

The `Provides`/`Consumes` edges and `ApiResource` are the tested bones; the contract-assignment is the new flesh. ITP501 stays retired but its spirit returns under a better model.

- **The minimal-model discipline cuts both ways.** ADR 0009 trimmed APIs precisely because nothing consumed them. The question to answer first is: *is there a real system now that needs to expose a synchronous/contract API to another system?* If it's still speculative, it fails the same test that got it cut.
- **`http` vs `asyncapi` shouldn't fork the concept.** An async interface already exists (topics). If an "API" can be asyncapi, you risk two ways to declare a message contract — `Publishes(topic)` and an asyncapi-backed API. Worth deciding whether asyncapi APIs *replace* the freeform topic declaration for cross-system contracts, leaving plain topics for intra-system edges.
- **Keep Microcks out of the public DSL**, as the mocks design already insists — the DSL says `FromOpenApi`/`FromAsyncApi`; the backend decides Microcks vs. real.

# System gateway APIs

## Summary

The topology gains a first-class **API** concept: the declared, contract-backed entry-point into a system — its *gateway* in the Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture sense. An API is defined by a machine-readable contract, either an **OpenAPI** document (synchronous request/response) or an **AsyncAPI** document (message-driven). Components inside the system *provide* an API; other systems and components *consume* it by its declared name, never by reaching a component directly.

The contract-assignment mechanism reuses the exact machinery already designed and built for platform-service development mocks (`development.Mock(...).FromOpenApi(...)`): declare an identity, attach a self-contained contract artifact, extract its identity, and let a backend stand an implementation behind the name. A development mock becomes the degenerate case of "provide an API whose backing implementation is a contract-only stub" — the same declaration, a different backend.

This reframes the API surface that the earlier full model carried as `ApiRef<T>` + `Provides`/`Consumes`. That surface was cut for being speculative and type-parameter-driven with no contract. The gateway reframing keeps the tested provider/consumer edges but grounds the concept in a contract, which is what makes it an API rather than a typed label.

No code changes are proposed by this document. It records the concept, the DSL shape, and the model so a future implementation starts from a decision rather than from memory.

## Context

The current minimal model declares three kinds of edge:

- **Async, system-internal or shared**: topics (`Publishes` / `Subscribes`). A topic is a freeform name plus a contract *type*; there is no message *document*.

- **Out to a platform service**: `Uses(ServiceRef)`, an external Dapr app identity with no contract in the topology; the contract lives only in a development mock.

What the model cannot express today is the *front door* of a system — the synchronous or message-driven interface another system is meant to call. Two gaps follow:

1. **No declared boundary.** Anything can, in principle, reach any component. The question "what does this system expose to the outside?" has no declarative answer, so it cannot be graphed, validated, or generated.
2. **No contract on the boundary.** The only contracts in the repository today are the OpenAPI mock artifacts under `examples/OrderFlow.SystemHost/mocks/`, and those describe *other* systems' services that order-flow *consumes*, not anything order-flow *provides*.

A **gateway** is the single entry-point into that collection: it "abstracts away the internal details of the domains – multiple services, data tables, ETL pipelines. The gateway's value — migration freedom, discoverability, reduced coupling — comes entirely from consumers depending on the interface, not the internals.

That is the meaning this design gives to *API* in the DSL: not "a typed reference," but "the system's declared gateway, backed by a contract."

## Goals

- Give a system a declared, graphable boundary: the set of APIs it provides to the outside.
- Make every provided API carry a machine-readable contract — OpenAPI or AsyncAPI.
- Let components consume an API by name, with the provider's internals hidden.
- Unify contract assignment with the existing `FromOpenApi` mock mechanism so one artifact pipeline serves both provided APIs and development mocks.
- Add AsyncAPI support so message-driven contracts are as first-class as synchronous ones.
- Keep Microcks, or any other backend, out of the public DSL.
- Preserve deterministic materialization, the per-block-builder compile-time-legality model, and the existing overlay/staging path.

## Non-goals

- Introducing a trigger concept or a `WorkloadType`; the API is a boundary, not an activation.
- Selecting or building an API-gateway runtime (Envoy, Kong, Dapr, YARP). The DSL declares the boundary; a backend fulfils it.

## Design principles

### An API is a contract, not a type

The document is the source of truth; the DSL only names it.

### Provide / consume are edges, and the consumer never names a component

A component *provides* an API. A component (in this system or another) *consumes* it by the API's declared name. The consumer's declaration is deliberately silent about which component serves it — that binding is the provider's private business and is exactly the freedom a gateway buys. {

```csharp
            .FromOpenApi("contracts/orders-api.openapi.yaml");

    // A message-driven gateway.
    public static readonly ApiRef OrderEvents =
        ApiRef.Define("order-events-api")
            .FromAsyncApi("contracts/order-events.asyncapi.yaml");
}
```

|---|---|---|

| `FromAsyncApi(path)` | AsyncAPI 2.x document | Message-driven (publish and/or subscribe operations) |

- no external `$ref`;
- non-empty `info.title`/`info.version`;

The API boundary is realized by the existing backends; the DSL introduces no new runtime primitive.

- **`generate`** emits, for a provided OpenAPI API, a Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` named for the API, scoped to its consumers, pointing at the provider's address (or, under a development mock, at Microcks) — reusing the endpoint-substitution mechanism already designed for service mocks. - **Aspire `run`** starts the provider and, when an API is mocked, imports its contract into the shared Microcks instance and gates the consumer on import readiness — the same task-backed readiness signal the service mocks use.

The keyword throughout is *reuse*: the API is a new declared edge, but it travels down pipelines that already exist.

New diagnostics follow the existing ITP pattern (codes assigned at implementation time; retired codes are not reused):

- An API name must be a valid DNS-1123 label (eager, at the call site, like other refs).
- A provided API must have at most one provider component; two components providing the same API is an error.
- A component may not provide and consume the same API.
- Only block kinds that can answer traffic may `Provides`; the builders make illegal kinds a compile error, with a validation backstop.
- An AsyncAPI API consumed for publish must be provided by a component that can publish; consumed for subscribe by a component that can subscribe — the consumer/provider operation directions must be compatible.
- A consumed API with no provider is a **warning**, not an error: a system may legitimately consume another system's gateway, whose provider is outside this topology. (Contrast with topics, where both sides must exist in-system — an API's whole point is to cross system boundaries.)

- Two provided APIs must not resolve to the same extracted contract identity (the duplicate-identity rule the mock builder already enforces).

The feature is additive. Existing systems declare no APIs and behave exactly as before: `Provides`/`Consumes`/`Apis` are empty, `graph` and `generate` emit nothing new, and no endpoint or readiness behavior changes. The mock mechanism is untouched; it only gains an overload.

Rejected. A generic type documents the contract to the compiler but cannot be published, stubbed, or contract-tested, and it was the speculative surface the minimal-model cut removed. A document-backed contract does everything the type did and more.

Rejected. Topics are freeform names with no message document; connectors are Dapr bindings to external systems. Neither expresses "a named, contract-backed interface another system calls." Forcing the concept into either would lose the contract and the provide/consume boundary.

Rejected, consistent with the mock design's refusal to name Microcks. The DSL declares a contract-backed boundary; whether a Dapr `HTTPEndpoint`, an ingress, or a stub fulfils it is a backend decision that should stay swappable.

### Require a provider for every consumed API

Rejected. An API is precisely the mechanism by which one system depends on another without sharing internals; requiring the provider in-topology would restrict APIs to a single system and recreate the coupling the gateway exists to remove. Hence a warning, not an error.

- **Query-style operations.** The DOMA gateway exposes "RPC APIs, messaging events and queries." Whether a read/query API is a distinct kind or just an OpenAPI GET is deferred; an OpenAPI document already covers it.

- [AsyncAPI specification](https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/latest) — the message-driven contract format.

- `docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md` — the `FromOpenApi` machinery this design builds on.

- An AsyncAPI API consumed for publish must be provided by a component that can publish; consumed for subscribe by a component that can subscribe — the consumer/provider operation directions must be compatible.
- A consumed API with no provider is a **warning**, not an error: a system may legitimately consume another system's gateway, whose provider is outside this topology. (Contrast with topics, where both sides must exist in-system — an API's whole point is to cross system boundaries.)
- Contract artifacts validate under the same rules as mock artifacts: existence, readability, self-containment, supported version, non-empty identity.
- Two provided APIs must not resolve to the same extracted contract identity (the duplicate-identity rule the mock builder already enforces).

## Compatibility and migration

The feature is additive. Existing systems declare no APIs and behave exactly as before: `Provides`/`Consumes`/`Apis` are empty, `graph` and `generate` emit nothing new, and no endpoint or readiness behavior changes. The mock mechanism is untouched; it only gains an overload.

The `full-topology` branch's tested provider/consumer edge machinery and snapshot expectations are the implementation starting point for the edges — but the contract-first `ApiRef` replaces its type-parameter `ApiRef<T>`, and the retired diagnostic code ITP501 is not revived.

## Alternatives considered

### Keep the type-parameter `ApiRef<T>`

Rejected. A generic type documents the contract to the compiler but cannot be published, stubbed, or contract-tested, and it was the speculative surface the minimal-model cut removed. A document-backed contract does everything the type did and more.

### Model a gateway as just another topic or connector

Rejected. Topics are freeform names with no message document; connectors are Dapr bindings to external systems. Neither expresses "a named, contract-backed interface another system calls." Forcing the concept into either would lose the contract and the provide/consume boundary.

### Expose the gateway runtime in the DSL

Rejected, consistent with the mock design's refusal to name Microcks. The DSL declares a contract-backed boundary; whether a Dapr `HTTPEndpoint`, an ingress, or a stub fulfils it is a backend decision that should stay swappable.

### Require a provider for every consumed API

Rejected. An API is precisely the mechanism by which one system depends on another without sharing internals; requiring the provider in-topology would restrict APIs to a single system and recreate the coupling the gateway exists to remove. Hence a warning, not an error.
